steps.title: Tinto Fino
steps.body: Ribera's grape is Tempranillo, locally called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. It has adapted to the extreme climate with thicker skins and smaller berries than in Rioja, giving darker, more concentrated wines with black fruit, liquorice and firm tannin. Reds must be at least 75% Tinto Fino; since 2019, rules allow 100% and blends with Cabernet, Merlot, Malbec, and white Albillo.
steps.highlight: Tinto Fino: thicker skins, darker wines

steps.title: Ageing
steps.body: Ribera uses Spain's ageing categories: Joven, Crianza, at least 24 months, 12 in oak; Reserva, 36 months, 12 in oak; Gran Reserva, 60 months, 24 in oak. Many wines use French oak and have a modern, powerful style. Since 2019, white wines from Albillo Mayor are also allowed as Ribera del Duero.

steps.explanation: Ribera's rules are close to Rioja's, with local names.

steps.body: Vega Sicilia's Único blends Tinto Fino with some Cabernet Sauvignon and ages for about ten years before release.

steps.prompt: How does Ribera's Tinto Fino typically compare with Rioja's Tempranillo?
steps.explanation: Thicker skins and extreme climate give power.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Tinto Fino is Ribera's Tempranillo, darker and more concentrated
Reds must be at least 75% Tinto Fino
Ribera uses Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva
